RagShortTexts: Once the splendid jewel of the Umayyad Caliphate, Córdoba served as a premier Christian.

Variants.Content: Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba in 1236, ending more than five centuries of Muslim rule over the city that had once been the capital of al-Andalus. The great mosque begun under Abd al-Rahman I, with its forest of red-and-white horseshoe arches, was consecrated as a cathedral soon after the conquest. Its old columns survived, and Gothic chapels were added along its walls over the following decades. The city stood on the Guadalquivir amid fertile olive plains, and its bridges and irrigated gardens made it a prize for any ruler who wished to hold the river valley. For centuries the city had been the place where Islamic learning and Christian frontier chivalry met, and the conquest turned that meeting point into a Christian stronghold.
Renowned Mudéjar tanners perfected supple cordovan leather, supplying elite European footwear and horse gear markets.
